title: I don't feel well
goal: Complain about feeling ill, name parts of the body, and meet a structure that flips the usual way of thinking: in Slovak, your head hurts you — you don't have a headache.
bekal: name parts of the body and say which one hurts
use *bolí ma* correctly — and know why it takes the accusative, not the dative
tell *je mi zle* from *bolí ma* and know when to use which

notes: **Bolí ma hlava** literally means "head hurts me". The **subject** of the sentence is the body part, and you are the **object** — in the accusative. The structure is like *páči sa mi* in unit 10, but the case is different: *páčiť sa* takes the dative, *boleť* takes the accusative. This is the most commonly confused pair in all of A1.

**Because the body part is the subject, the verb agrees with it.** *Bolí ma hlava* (one head), but *Bolia ma nohy* (my legs hurt, plural) and *Bolia ma zuby* (my teeth hurt). Use a singular verb for a body part that comes in pairs and your sentence sounds odd.

**Nie je mi dobre** takes the dative — here we're talking about how you feel overall, not one part that hurts. Compare: *Bolí ma hlava* (one spot, accusative) and *Je mi zle* (the whole body, dative). Two structures, two cases, two clearly different jobs.

**Je mi zima** isn't "I am cold" but "to me it is cold". All bodily feelings follow this pattern: *je mi teplo* (I'm hot), *je mi zle* (I feel sick), *je mi smutno* (I'm sad), *je mi to jedno* (it's all the same to me).

**Otvorte, povedzte, pite, odpočívajte** — all polite commands, ending in *-te*. You don't need to produce them at A1, but you must recognize them: every instruction you get from a doctor, an official, or a shop assistant will use this form.

grammars.title: Bolí ma — the structure that flips the subject
body: English makes the person the subject: "I have a headache". Slovak makes the body part the subject: "head hurts me". Once you accept that flip, the whole table becomes easy.
after: **The pronoun is accusative** — the same forms as unit 4: *ma, ťa, ho, ju, nás, vás, ich*. Compare *páčiť sa*, which takes *mi, ti, mu, jej, nám, vám, im*. If you get mixed up, remember this tag line: **"head hurts** me**"** — hurting has an object, and objects take the accusative.
**In the past, the ending follows the body part**: *Bolela ma hlava* (f), *Bolelo ma brucho* (n), *Boleli ma nohy* (plural). Once again the body part is the subject, so the ending follows its gender.

**If in doubt, there's a way out that's always right:** *Mám bolesti hlavy* ("I have head pains") uses a structure that feels natural to your ear and is still correct Slovak. It's a little more formal, but never wrong.

grammars.title: Je mi … — feelings that affect the whole body
body: When what you feel isn't pain in one spot but an overall state, Slovak uses *je mi* + an adverb, with the **dative**.

head: Slovak
Literally
English
rows: I feel sick; I don't feel well.
It's all the same to me.

after: **The last row comes up a lot.** *Je mi ľúto* is how you offer condolences, and also how you say no politely: *Je mi ľúto, ale nemôžem* = "I'm sorry, but I can't".
**Notice that the word after *mi* never changes form.** *Zle, dobre, zima, teplo, smutno* are all fixed adverbs. You don't need to match anything to your gender.
**The past:** replace *je* with *bolo* — *Bolo mi zle*, *Bolo mi zima*. The future: *Bude mi zle*. Change one word, and the whole pattern follows.

blocks.text: **Oko → oči and ucho → uši** are irregular plurals, both left over from an old form for "two things" that has disappeared from modern Slovak. Because eyes and ears always come in pairs, the form survived right here.

blocks.title: Four words with no vowels
items: *Krk* (neck), *prst* (finger), *chrbát* (back, its first syllable), *smrť* (death) — body parts give Slovak some of its most famous vowel-less words.
How to say them: let the *r* carry the syllable, with only the faintest hint of a vowel before it — krk, prst, KHR-baht. Don't add a full vowel — that instantly sounds foreign.

sections.title: At the doctor's and the pharmacy

blocks.text: **Uzdrav sa!** (informal) or **Uzdravte sa!** (polite) is what you say to someone who is ill. When someone sneezes, say **Na zdravie!** — the same phrase used for a toast.

blocks.title: Healthcare in Slovakia
items: International students and registered workers must have *zdravotné poistenie* (health insurance). With the card, a visit to a general practitioner is practically free.

A *lekáreň* (pharmacy) sells many medicines without a prescription, and the pharmacist is usually happy to hear your symptoms and suggest something — often a faster first step than queuing at a clinic.
*Pohotovosť* is the emergency service, open outside working hours. Emergency numbers: **112** for everything, **155** for an ambulance.
I have a fever and a cough.
